inlines.text: Jordan Schneider

blocks.text: On Monday, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang, eleven days after he resigned over his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, saying it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government." Midway through our recording, the Commerce Department finally put Megaspeed on the Entity List — and Chris read it live.

inlines.text: On Monday, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang, eleven days after he resigned over his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, saying it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government." Midway through our recording, the Commerce Department finally put Megaspeed on the Entity List — and Chris read it live.

blocks.text: Joining me for an emergency pod are Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations and former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the NSC, and Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown's Institute of International Economic Law, host of Security Economics, and Biden's former senior director for international economics.

inlines.text: Joining me for an emergency pod are Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations and former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the NSC, and Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown's Institute of International Economic Law, host of
Security Economics

blocks.text: We discuss…

inlines.text: We discuss…
What Trump promised Nvidia
— pardons, sweetheart settlements, or future licenses, and why a five-year statute of limitations means the board wants its past buttoned up.
Policy by stock ticker
— how last week's selloff drove the reversal, and why it will add volatility rather than tamp it down.
American state capitalism
— a president picking the CEO of one of America's most valuable companies, and the PRC parallels.
What Congress can and can't do
— why AI Overwatch, MATCH, and RASA don't touch smuggling, and the case for laws that compel license denials.
The Entity List, live
— Chris reads the Megaspeed listing on air and finds no foreign direct product rule attached.
Palace intrigue
— Bessent and Rubio's missed shot at Lutnick, and why oversight will have to come from the Hill.

blocks.text: Two things seem plausible to me. One is forgiveness for past sins. I obviously don't know exactly what was going on inside Nvidia — I only know the press reports — but I think it's plausible that Nvidia, including its executives, might have quite a bit of liability around past export-control violations, right up to today. Did Trump say he'd pardon them, or do a settlement on very favorable terms? What did he promise to resolve the past violations?

blocks.text: The other important question is what he's promised for the future. We know for a fact that BIS at the Commerce Department had already been issuing Nvidia licenses to export chips to China. Putting aside the smuggling, they were also getting licenses. Have they made soft or firm commitments about future licenses? There's quite a bit the president of the United States can promise Nvidia out of this transaction, and while it's bad for US national security, he clearly dangled something that made this attractive.

blocks.text: One final point. If I were Nvidia, I would want the past violations buttoned up. I'd want either a pardon or a settlement, because export-control violations carry a five-year statute of limitations. If Trump simply puts the investigation on ice, the next president can pick it back up and impose liability. But if Trump pardons or does a settlement on extremely favorable terms, that gives Nvidia final resolution of its potential legal — albeit not political — problems.

blocks.text: The question everyone is asking right now is, first, why wasn't Commerce enforcing the controls that should have prevented the shipments to Megaspeed? And second, can we trust Commerce to enforce the controls they just put on — which would nominally prevent shipments to companies like Megaspeed — in a way that's serious and robust and actually accomplishes that objective? If the answer is no, then Congress needs legislation that takes the keys away from them and says you are compelled to deny licenses in X, Y, and Z circumstances, or to these countries. It's going to have to get a lot more specific, and that's probably something for the next Congress. I don't think there's time here.
